description:
ML tool to find Earth analogs for the Moon and Mars

We're searching Earth for locations that resemble candidate Moon base sites (Mars landing sites as a stretch goal).

- Per-factor scoring on terrain, temperature and geology, not one overall score

- Shows where the analogy holds and where it breaks down

- Interactive map with a breakdown for every site

Stack: Python, machine learning, geospatial analysis, NASA open data
summary: ATLAS (Analog Terrain & Lunar Alignment System) finds the places on Earth where NASA can test its future permanent Moon bases. We profiled all four planned lunar polar base sites, Peary, Shackleton, de Gerlache and Amundsen, from real NASA LRO data (LOLA terrain, Diviner temperatures, shadow and illumination maps), then profiled 14 lesser-known extreme Earth locations across six terrain types with exactly the same measurements, using ESA Copernicus DEM, NASA POWER and SoilGrids data. A transparent weighted model scores every base-site pair, and a live mission-control web app lets anyone explore the rankings, re-weight them by mission type, and compare sites side by side. ATLAS turns analog-site selection from hand cross-referencing into a ranked, repeatable shortlist, and discovers new candidate sites instead of re-listing the famous ones.
details:
WHAT ATLAS DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

NASA plans permanent bases at four lunar polar craters: Peary, Shackleton, de Gerlache and Amundsen. Before hardware and crews go there, they must be tested on Earth, at places that behave the same way. ATLAS finds those places. We measured all four Moon bases from real NASA LRO data, both poles, not just the south: elevation, slope, flat area, surface roughness, permanently shadowed area, sun and Earth visibility, and Diviner temperatures down to -184 °C to -224 °C. We then profiled 14 lesser-known extreme Earth locations across six terrain types (arid basins, salt flats, volcanic fields, lava tubes, permafrost and impact craters) with exactly the same statistics. Every base-site pair (56 in total) receives an Analog Score from five weighted pillars fixed in advance: slope 30%, flat area 20%, temperature 20%, soil 15%, relief 15%. The same method also profiles Mars, Jezero Crater from MGS MOLA data.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Analog-site selection today means hand cross-referencing siloed datasets and defaulting to a few famous sites. ATLAS replaces that with a ranked, repeatable shortlist backed by traceable measurements, delivered in a live mission-control web app where planners can re-weight the scores by mission type (Rover, Habitat, ISRU) and compare any base-site pair side by side on a radar chart.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Data: NASA LRO LOLA, Diviner and illumination/PSR products (PDS/PGDA), MGS MOLA, NASA POWER, ESA Copernicus DEM GLO-30, SoilGrids 2.0. Built with Python (rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, scikit-learn, including a custom PDS3 parser, because GDAL ships no PDS driver), a FastAPI backend, a vanilla JavaScript and Leaflet frontend, and a Streamlit version; deployed on Vercel, code open on GitHub.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Instead of re-ranking the famous analogs, we first validated our untuned engine on them. It reproduced the literature's own answers (McMurdo first for three bases, Atacama first for Peary). Then we excluded them and ran a discovery search that produced new results: de Gerlache to Mount Erebus, Antarctica (72.1); Shackleton to Klyuchevskaya Volcanic Group, Russia (69.7); Peary to Elgygytgyn Crater, Russia (63.1); Amundsen to Mount Erebus (62.7).

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy before scoring: we caught and corrected real errors in the source data. The north-pole grid was flipped (proven by a crater test), Shackleton's IAU centre sits on the crater rim (89.67°S, 129.78°E), Amundsen lies outside the standard south-pole mosaic, and no-data cells were corrupting its slope (15.2° corrected to 10.3°). Honesty throughout: sun and Earth visibility are reported but never scored (they have no Earth counterpart), and values that could not be measured are marked missing, never estimated. Limitations are stated openly: no Earth site matches lunar polar cold, Moon data is 240 m against Earth's 30 m, and the pool is a curated shortlist, not a global scan. A global scan, cave LiDAR geometry and LEND/M3 water-ice layers are our next steps.
dataRefs: LRO LOLA Gridded Data Records (LDEM/LDSM/LDRM) — Moon polar elevation, slope, roughness
LRO LOLA Permanently Shadowed Region Maps (LPSR)
LRO Diviner Polar Cumulative Products (PCP) — bolometric temperature, both poles
Lunar Illumination & Average Visibility Maps (Mazarico et al.) — Sun and Earth visibility
NASA PGDA — LOLA Polar Products Catalog (South Pole mosaic, 80S and North Pole DEMs)
MGS MOLA MEGDR — Mars topography (Jezero Crater)
NASA POWER Climatology API — Earth site temperatures
projectRefs: Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (ESA / Airbus) — Earth elevation
SoilGrids 2.0 (ISRIC) — sand, clay and coarse-fragment fractions
Google Maps Embedded Tiles — basemap imagery in the web app
